opening.headline: Learn how to absorb limit exceedances through design so that the entire service does not stop when an external model slows down or exceeds its limits.
body: Let's consider our service makes asynchronous calls to an external model API for each request. If the external model responds slowly or returns a 429 limit-exceeded error, the thread making the call continues to wait. As the number of waiting requests accumulates, non-model-related functionality also becomes sluggish.

Since capacity overages and delays can occur at any time, they must be addressed during the design phase, not after a failure has occurred. In this class, we examine how capacity limits and delays differ based on Databricks' capacity model, and we distinguish among retry, fallback, queuing, and circuit breaker strategies depending on specific scenarios. Finally, we explore the process of selecting appropriate handling mechanisms based on request characteristics in the case where the 429 error rate suddenly increases.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This can explain the effects of rate limiting and serving capacity on limits and delay.
You can distinguish and select appropriate mechanisms such as retry, fallback, queuing, and circuit breaker based on the situation.

screens.title: If the external model becomes slow, the entire service becomes slow.
screens.lead: First, let's examine the scenario where delay from an external model propagates throughout the entire service. Follow the diagram to see where pending requests accumulate.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the service calling an external model, causing response delays that accumulate pending requests and block other functionalities.
labels: Performance degradation occurs even for features unrelated to the model.

paragraphs: Our service calls the external model API whenever a user request is received. This is normally fine. However, it begins to experience slow responses from the external model or returns 429 errors indicating rate limit exceeded.

The thread invoked is blocked, waiting for a response. Requests continue to arrive, but since the thread does not release, pending requests accumulate. Eventually, even functionalities unrelated to model calls—such as login or search—become sluggish. As a result, one external dependency has become the determining factor for the overall service performance.

Overdraft or delays may occur. Therefore, instead of reacting after an incident has happened, mechanisms to absorb such issues should be established during the design phase. This course covers the roles and selection criteria for rate limiting, retrying, fallback models, and queuing.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The slowdown is due to external issues, but the effect spreading across the entire service is our design's problem. Consider where the spread can be halted and follow along.

screens.outro: First, let's recall what alternatives are available for our current service.

screens.title: Do we have an alternative in case of external API failures?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please click it first to see what our service offers, without entering an answer yet.

items.prompt: Can the same request be sent to a different model or a different provider?
items.answer: When the primary model continues to fail, there must be an alternative pathway to route requests, preventing service disruption. This alternative pathway is called a fallback. Since the alternative model may differ in quality or cost, it is essential to predefine the acceptable level of difference.

items.prompt: Can non-urgent requests be processed later?
items.answer: Work that does not require immediate responses can be held in a queue and processed at a pace matching the processing speed. This approach ensures stable processing within limits while maintaining capacity available for real-time requests. This method is known as queuing.

items.prompt: How many retries are you performing, and what interval are you using?
items.answer: Retry is effective for transient failures, but immediate and continuous retry exacerbates the situation by increasing pressure on limits. Exponential backoff with a limited number of retries is the default approach. If neither the number of retries nor the interval is predefined, it becomes a risk factor.

screens.outro: Since we've come up with an alternative, let's examine the source of the limit separately by capacity type.

screens.title: Rate limiting and serving capacity: Where does the limit come from?
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how consistency of delay and capacity guarantees, as well as pricing, differ based on the billing method.

tabs.label: rate limit
tabs.body: Rate limiting refers to the maximum number of requests allowed by the provider or endpoint. When this limit is exceeded, requests are typically rejected or delayed, and rejections are usually indicated by errors such as 429. Since this limit is set externally and is independent of our service design, we must define how to handle cases where the limit is exceeded.

tabs.label: pay-per-token
tabs.body: The pay-per-token model of Databricks Foundation Model APIs is the easiest way to get started. You can immediately use pre-configured endpoints. However, since it operates on standard best-effort traffic, latency may vary under load. While suitable for initial use, it may be insufficient for latency-sensitive operational workloads.

tabs.label: priority pay-per-token
tabs.body: A pay-per-token feature designed for latency-sensitive real-time applications. If the request specifies the `service_tier` parameter as `priority`, it is processed before standard best-effort traffic and achieves more consistent latency even under load. This option is selected per request and incurs higher token pricing without requiring a contract.

tabs.label: provisioned throughput
tabs.body: Recommended approach for workloads requiring high throughput and performance guarantees, fine-tuned models, and additional security requirements. Two options are available: on-demand (without commitments) and reserved instances (with fixed-term commitments) to secure dedicated capacity. Dedicated capacity is selected when performance guarantees are needed.

tabs.label: Auto Scaling and Cold Start
tabs.body: Model serving scales up or down automatically based on demand. However, when scale-to-zero is enabled and the endpoint is not in use, cold start delays occur upon receiving new requests, and capacity is not guaranteed during that state. Therefore, it is not recommended for operational endpoints.

screens.outro: Since we have verified the source of the limit, let's now examine the flow of devices that absorb when the limit is exceeded.

screens.title: Retry, fallback model, queuing, and circuit breaker
screens.lead: When you select the image number marker, you can view detailed information. Follow the flow from step 1 as it goes through the router, splitting into the base model, alternative model, and queue.

visual.alt: A flow diagram where the request flows through the router, splitting into the base model, alternative model, and queue.

markers.label: Router
markers.title: Determine where to send the request
markers.body: The router determines where to send a request based on the nature of the request and the current state of the base model. If the base model is healthy, the request is forwarded directly; if failures occur, it is routed to an alternative path. Traffic can be distributed among multiple models hosted on a single serving endpoint, allowing alternative paths to reside within the same endpoint. External models can also be connected to a centralized endpoint under Databricks governance, making it easy to switch providers.

markers.label: Retry
markers.title: Transient failure triggers backup retry
markers.body: Retries are appropriate only for transient failures that momentarily exceed limits. A backoff strategy that increases intervals and limits the number of attempts is required. Immediately retrying when limits are exceeded will worsen the situation, and retrying beyond the time a user is willing to wait becomes meaningless.

markers.label: Circuit Breaker
markers.title: Fails consecutively, the call itself is terminated.
markers.body: A circuit breaker stops calling the default model entirely for a set period of time after consecutive failures and immediately sends the request to a fallback. By not waiting for responses from failed calls, it prevents a buildup of pending requests that would otherwise slow down the entire system. After the specified time has elapsed, it attempts the call again to verify whether recovery has occurred.

markers.label: fallback model
markers.title: Alternative path when the base model continues to fail
markers.body: A fallback model redirects requests to an alternative model or alternative provider when the primary model continues to fail. The service does not need to be down; instead, quality or cost may differ, and this approach should only be used when the differences are acceptable. Capacity must also be reserved for the alternative path.

markers.label: Queuing
markers.title: Requests that do not require immediate response are queued.
markers.body: Queuing holds requests that do not require immediate responses in a queue and forwards them at a pace matching the processing speed. It is designed to accommodate tasks that can tolerate delays, processing them stably within defined limits. However, it is not suitable for real-time requests that require immediate responses due to significant latency. Note that route optimization improves latency and throughput, but it does not replace the limits set by the provider.

screens.outro: Since we confirmed that the appropriate scenarios vary by device, let's apply this to cases where the 429 ratio has increased.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Conditions under which fallback is required when 429 increases
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down a case where the ratio of 429 suddenly increased, step by step. Select the next arrow to learn about the cause and proceed through the process of choosing the device based on the nature of the request.

visual.alt: 429 Decision tree that splits based on duration and request characteristics into retry, circuit breaker and fallback, or queuing when ratio increases.
labels: Do you need a direct answer?
Condition: Alternative model quality acceptable, alternative path capacity secured

steps.title: Situation: 429 ratio increased from 1% to 20%
steps.body: The real-time chatbot calls an external model. The 429 error rate, which normally occurs at around 1%, increased to 20%. Since the agent is in the middle of a conversation with the user, they cannot wait for an extended period.

steps.title: Stage 1: Cause Classification
steps.body: First, it determines whether the issue is temporary or persistent based on duration. If the condition resolves within a few seconds, it is temporary; if the ratio does not decrease even after several minutes, it is persistent. This distinction will determine the subsequent device selection.

steps.title: Step 2: Temporary failure, retry backup
steps.body: If temporary, it is absorbed by retrying backup. Retries are performed only within a delay that users can tolerate. For example, attempt up to three times with increasing intervals; if still unsuccessful, proceed to the next device.

steps.title: If three steps persist, trigger circuit breaker and fallback
steps.body: If it persists, retries further increase pressure on the limit. The circuit breaker stops basic model calls and redirects requests to an alternative model. Since calls are halted, no accumulated requests remain, preventing delays from spreading across the entire service.

steps.title: Step 4: If the task does not require immediate response, queue it.
steps.body: Even with the same model, requests that do not require immediate responses are fundamentally different. Such requests are queued and processed gradually within defined limits. This also helps maintain the resource capacity required for real-time chatbots.

steps.title: Conditions for using step 5 fallback
steps.body: Fallback is used only when all three conditions are met: the request must be real-time, the quality of the alternative model must be within acceptable limits, and sufficient capacity must be available on the alternative path. If any one of these conditions is not satisfied, the alternative path may instead become a new bottleneck.

steps.title: Conclusion: Different devices depending on the nature of the request
steps.body: Exceeding limits is handled differently by various devices depending on the nature of the request—whether it is real-time or non-real-time—and whether the failure is temporary or persistent. Attempting to handle all cases with a single device may actually worsen the situation in some cases.

screens.outro: We have completed the example; now I will summarize the key points and conclude.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Overlimit is absorbed by design.
screens.lead: Summarize the course content with a single criterion. Review it by recalling the accumulating queue in the opening scene.

paragraphs: Overdraft and delays are possible, so they are absorbed in the design. Each device has its own specific circumstances. Retries are appropriate for transient failures, fallbacks for persistent failures, and queuing for requests where immediate responses are not required. A circuit breaker stops calls when failures persist, preventing failure accumulation from cascading across the entire service.

Capacity options have different limits and latency characteristics. Pay-per-token is easy to start with, but latency can vary under load. Priority pay-per-token prioritizes requests that specify `service_tier`, at a higher unit price. Provisioned throughput is recommended for production workloads requiring performance guarantees. Scale to zero is unsuitable for production endpoints because it introduces cold-start latency and does not guarantee capacity.

When making a choice, ask two questions first: Does this request require an immediate response? And is the failure transient or persistent? Based on the answers to these two questions, the appropriate mechanism—retry, circuit breaker, fallback, or queuing—is determined.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: To use fallback, the quality of the alternative model must be within acceptable limits and the capacity of the alternative path must be secured. Ensure in advance that the alternative path does not become a new bottleneck.

checks.intro: Please verify the selection criteria you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: The external model continuously returns limit exceeded (429) errors. What would be appropriate for a real-time chatbot?
options: Attempts immediate retry repeatedly without backoff
Circuit breakers halt calls and route them to a fallback model with acceptable quality
Queues all requests for slow, sequential processing
Turn on scale to zero to increase the limit.
checks.explain: In continuous failures, retries further stress the limits, so the call is terminated and fallback is used to prevent accumulation of pending requests.

wrong.0: Exceeding the limit and immediately retrying will make the situation worse.
wrong.2: Queuing responds to requests without immediate answers, while real-time chatbots experience significant delays.
wrong.3: Scale to zero incurs cold start delays and does not guarantee capacity.

checks.intro: Organize by the nature of the request and the device. The result is not recorded.
checks.q: Match the nature of the request with the appropriate device.
left: No need for immediate response, like a summary deployment.
checks.explain: Transient failures should be retried, persistent failures should use a circuit breaker with fallback, non-real-time requests should be queued, and when guarantees are needed, provisioned throughput is the right solution.

glossary.def: This is the rate limit per unit time allowed by the provider or endpoint. If exceeded, the request is rejected or delayed.
An alternative model that handles requests instead of the base model when the base model continues to fail.
This is a method where requests that do not require immediate responses are queued and sent out at a pace matching the processing speed.
This is a retry policy that gradually increases the retry interval and limits the number of retries.
A device that stops periodic calls after a series of failures and forwards the call to an alternative path to prevent accumulation of pending calls.

misconceptions.myth: Just retry immediately if it fails.
misconceptions.fact: If immediate repetition occurs within a limit, it further pressures the limit and worsens the situation. The interval should be increased and the number of repetitions should be limited.

misconceptions.myth: If you run it through the fallback model, the quality is the same.
misconceptions.fact: Replacement models may differ in quality and cost. It is essential to pre-determine whether you can accept these differences and to ensure sufficient capacity for the alternative path.

misconceptions.myth: Queuing can be used for all requests.
misconceptions.fact: Queuing matches requests that can wait. It does not match real-time requests that require immediate responses due to long waiting times.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Overdraft and delay are absorbed at the design stage.
Retries are for transient failures, fallbacks are for persistent failures, and queuing is for requests where immediate responses are not required.
A circuit breaker prevents accumulated latency from propagating across the entire service.
Pay-per-token, priority, and provisioned throughput have different limits and latency characteristics.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When our service causes an external model to become slow or returns a 429, what do users see, and what alternative paths are available?
